items.readable_text:
Content:
We can use the standard algorithm to multiply two-digit numbers.

Content:
To illustrate, let's use the standard algorithm to compute [MATH: 12\times 13.]

Content:
Recall that [MATH: {\color{blue}1}{\color{red}3}] in expanded form is [MATH: {\color{blue}10} + {\color{red}3}.] The idea is to first multiply [MATH: 12] by [MATH: {\color{red}3},] then by [MATH: {\color{blue}10},] and add the results.

Content:
We write one number above the other as follows:

Content:
[MATH: 1|2; ×|0|0|1|3|36 + 120 = 156]

Content:
First, we multiply the top number ([MATH: 12]) by the value in the ones place of the second number ([MATH: \bbox[2px, lightgray]{3}]), writing the result under the line:

Content:
[MATH: 1|2; ×|0|0|1|3; 3|6|12 × 3 = 36000]

Content:
Next, we multiply [MATH: 12] by [MATH: \bbox[2px, lightgray]{1}0.] Let's do this in steps:

Content:
Step 1: Any number multiplied by [MATH: 10] always gives a zero at the end. Therefore, we place a zero in the ones column underneath our first result.

Content:
[MATH: 1|2; ×|0|0|1|3; 3|6; 0|12 × 10 = 1200]

Content:
Step 2: Now, we work out [MATH: \bbox[2px, lightgray]{2}\times \bbox[2px, lightgray]{1}.] We place the answer next to our zero:

Content:
[MATH: 1|2; ×|0|0|1|3; 3|6; 2|0|2 × 1 = 20]

Content:
Step 3: Next, we we work out [MATH: \bbox[2px, lightgray]{1}\times \bbox[2px, lightgray]{1}]:

Content:
[MATH: 1|2; ×|0|0|1|3; 3|6; 1|2|0|1 × 1 = 10]

Content:
Finally, we add the results:

Content:
[MATH: 1|2; ×|0|0|1|3; 3|6; +|1|2|0; 1|5|6|36 + 120 = 156]

Content:
Therefore, [MATH: 12 \times 13 = 156.]

Content:
Just like when multiplying a number by a one-digit number, we will sometimes have carries. Let's see how to deal with this by multiplying [MATH: 24] by [MATH: 32.]

Content:
We write it this way:

Content:
[MATH: 2|4; ×|0|0|3|2|48 + 720 = 768]

Content:
First, we multiply the ones:

Content:
[MATH: 0; [math]\color{blue}\phantom{0}[/math]; 2|4; ×|0|0|3|2; 4|8|24 × 2 = 48000]

Content:
On this occasion, there were no carries when multiplying the ones, and so the carry box [MATH: 0] remains empty.

Content:
Next, we multiply the tens. Let's do this in steps.

Content:
Step 1: We start by writing a zero:

Content:
[MATH: 0; [math]\color{blue}\phantom{0}[/math]; 2|4; ×|0|0|3|2; 4|8; 0|24 × 30 = 7200]

Content:
Step 2: We now work out [MATH: \bbox[2px, lightgray]{4}\times \bbox[2px, lightgray]{3} = {\color{blue}1}{\color{red}2}.] We carry the [MATH: {\color{blue}1}] and write down [MATH: \color{red}2]:

Content:
[MATH: [math]\color{blue}1[/math]; [math]\color{blue}\phantom{0}[/math]; 2|4; ×|0|0|3|2; 4|8; 2|0|4 × 3 = 12; Carry:1; Write:2]

Content:
Step 3: We multiply [MATH: \bbox[2px, lightgray]{2}\times \bbox[2px, lightgray]{3} = 6,] and we add the carry from the previous multiplication to make [MATH: 6+{\color{blue}{1}} = {\color{red}{7}}.]

Content:
[MATH: [math]\color{blue}1[/math]; [math]\color{blue}\phantom{0}[/math]; 2|4; ×|0|0|3|2; 4|8; 7|2|0|2 × 3 = 6and6 + 1 = 7; Carry: −; Write:7]

Content:
Finally, we add the results:

Content:
[MATH: [math]\color{blue}1[/math]; [math]\color{blue}\phantom{0}[/math]; 2|4; ×|0|0|3|2; 4|8; +|7|2|0; 7|6|8|48 + 720 = 768]

Content:
Therefore, [MATH: 24 \times 32 = 768.]
